factChecks.claim: Passkeys use cryptographic key pairs; servers retain public keys, and credentials are linked to the app or website for which they were created.
The best security feature can also remove product friction rather than merely adding warnings.

angle: security that removes a user task
shareValue: A three-question test for whether a security change also improves the product experience.
problemStatement: Passwords make users create, remember, protect, and repeatedly enter a reusable secret.
solutionStatement: Passkeys replace the reusable password with cryptographic key pairs linked to the real app or website.

verifiedFacts: Passkeys replace passwords with cryptographic key pairs based on FIDO Alliance and W3C standards.
Servers retain public keys rather than password secrets.
Passkeys are linked to the app or website for which they were created, making them resistant to phishing.
Apple supports sign-in with AutoFill and Face ID or Touch ID.
editorialBrief.analysis: Passkeys are an example of security and usability improving together because the user no longer has to create, remember, or type a password.
doNotClaim: Do not call any authentication system unhackable.
Do not imply passkeys remove all account-recovery or rollout work.

captions.instagram:
The best security upgrade can remove a job from the user.

Apple explains that passkeys replace passwords with cryptographic key pairs. Servers retain public keys, and a passkey is linked to the app or website for which it was created—making it resistant to phishing.

The product lesson is bigger than authentication: better security does not always require more user effort. But rollout still needs a clear recovery path and a transition for people using passwords. Save the final slide for your next account-flow review.
